title: Running containers with docker run
idea: `docker run` creates a container from an image and starts it. Flags before the image name choose how it runs.
points: By default `docker run` stays attached: the app's output fills your terminal.
A command after the image name replaces the image's `CMD`, its default start command.
`-e NAME=value` sets an environment variable; the Book Store API reads `PORT` this way.
`--rm` deletes the container when it exits, which suits one-off commands.

code.caption: Two long-running containers, two one-off commands, then cleanup.

walk.text: Start `api` in the background. Port 3000 on your host reaches port 3000 in the container.
A second container. `-e PORT=4000` makes the app listen on 4000, so publish 4000.
A command after the image name replaces the default. It prints Node's version; `--rm` then cleans up.
`-it` gives you an interactive shell in a fresh container; `--rm` removes it on exit.
Stop both containers by name. They stay on disk, still holding their names.
Remove them. A name can be reused only after its container is removed.

pitfalls: Put flags before the image name; after it, `-d` becomes part of the container's command.
Reusing `--name api` fails while any container, even stopped, holds it; remove that one first.
Keep real secrets out of committed scripts; load them with `--env-file` from an untracked file.

quiz.why: Text after the image name replaces the default command, so `node --version` runs instead of the server. `--rm` removes the container when it exits.

takeaway: Shape the run with flags; pick the program with what follows the image.
